findings.title: SQL injection (string concat)
findings.description: SQL query built with string interpolation may allow SQL injection.
findings.why: String-interpolated queries let user input become part of the SQL grammar. That's every SQL-injection tutorial ever, and it still ends companies.
findings.snippet: const result = await client.query(`SELECT COUNT(*)::bigint AS count FROM public."${tableName}"`);
findings.fix: Use parameterized queries or an ORM with prepared statements.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a secret — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce secret. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.title: Sensitive data logged to console

findings.fix: Remove logging of sensitive fields or redact them.

findings.title: Math.random() used for security-sensitive value
findings.description: Math.random() appears to be used for non-security tracking, UI, correlation, delay, animation, or logging identifiers.
findings.why: Math.random() is a predictable pseudo-random generator seeded from clock/context. An attacker who sees a few outputs can predict the next one — fine for animation, catastrophic for tokens or OTPs.
findings.snippet: const applyRetryJitter = (delayMs: number): number => Math.floor(delayMs * (0.5 + Math.random()));
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() instead.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a token — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce token. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker. Found in test file — likely intentional test fixture. Verify this is not a real credential.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').
